sections.h2: What sets University City sales apart
sections.html:
University City is an inner-ring suburb of St. Louis in St. Louis County, and its housing is older than most of the county around it. One city rule touches every seller: a house sold or rented here needs a city occupancy permit before anyone moves in, and the city suggests arranging the inspection before you list. Plan for that step early, because it shapes repairs, timing and what a buyer, whether a family or an investor, has to do after closing.

The 2020 census found 35,065 residents. The July 2025 estimate is 34,657, a dip of 1.6 percent. Streetcar-era blocks in the south and postwar blocks in the north sit within a few miles of each other, so condition and layout vary from one street to the next.

The southern part of the city, especially around Delmar Boulevard, keeps much of its historic architecture. The northern part developed mostly after World War II, with shopping centers and more car-oriented streets. A buyer looking at a 1920s house south of Delmar is comparing different things than a buyer looking at a postwar house north of Olive, so describe yours accurately.

City Hall is at 6801 Delmar Boulevard in the former Magazine Building, a 135-foot tower. The School District of University City runs the public schools, including University City High School. Name the district in your listing, since families often search by district.

Owners live in 56.2 percent of homes, which leaves a sizable rental stock and a steady flow of landlord buyers. That is why the city's occupancy rules for rentals and sales get so much attention.

Plan on one. Anyone moving into University City must apply for and receive an occupancy permit before moving in, and anyone planning to sell should arrange an inspection before the house goes on the market. The inspection fee for a home sale is $80 per unit.

  • File with Planning and Zoning on the fourth floor of City Hall, 6801 Delmar Boulevard, or email inspections@ucitymo.org.
  • The application fee is $25 and is not refundable. Card payments carry a 3.25 percent convenience fee.
  • Inspectors check electrical, plumbing, heating and general building condition against the property maintenance code.
  • A valid driver's license, state ID or passport is accepted as identification.

If the house fails, the city requires corrections. For minor repairs it may issue a conditional occupancy permit for $35, which gives the owner 60 days to finish the work while people live there. Miss that 60-day mark and the city may notify owner and residents that occupancy is no longer valid, and legal action can follow.

sections.h2: Sale routes for a University City house
sections.html:
You can go through an agent, sell the house yourself, or accept an offer from an investor who buys houses in their current state. Each runs into the same occupancy requirement, so ask each buyer who will order the inspection and who pays for repairs.

  • List on the market. You pay the inspection fee, fix what the inspector flags, and ask your agent for the commission rate and the likely closing timeline.
  • Sell it yourself. You save an agent's fee but handle pricing, showings, the contract and the city paperwork.
  • Sell to an investor. A buyer paying cash is not waiting on a lender. Weigh each offer against what a listing would leave you after repairs, the inspection and closing costs.

Houses with a failed inspection, a holdover tenant or an estate still in probate are harder to list. Those are the situations where investor offers tend to come up. Get at least two written offers and read what each says about who pays closing costs.

Walk the house before the inspector does. Test every outlet and switch you can reach, run the taps and the shower, and make sure the furnace fires. The inspector reviews electrical, plumbing, heating and overall condition, so loose railings, exposed wiring and leaks are the usual trouble spots.

Book the visit early and leave time for repairs. A failed inspection is not the end of a sale, but it adds a second visit and, if you take the conditional route, a 60-day clock. A seller who finds problems first can fix them on a schedule instead of under pressure.

sections.h2: Selling with a tenant in place
sections.html:
A tenant complicates the occupancy permit, because the permit is tied to whoever lives in the house. Read the lease for its end date, then tell the tenant in writing once you have a contract. Ask the city what a buyer must file after closing, and give the buyer the lease and rent history if the tenant is staying.

When a tenant refuses access, an inspection can stall. Investors who buy rentals often accept the house with the tenant in place and handle the permit themselves, which is one reason landlords look at cash offers.

St. Louis County, not the city, bills the tax: the Assessor sets the value and the Collector of Revenue collects. The bill for a year is on time if paid or postmarked by December 31. After that, interest of up to 18 percent a year plus a 2 percent penalty can apply under RSMo chapters 139 and 140.

State law has the Assessor revalue every parcel in odd-numbered years, and 2027 is the next one. Appeals go to the independent Board of Equalization, and filing runs from May 1 through the second Monday in July. The next window opens May 1, 2027. The Collector's office is at 41 S. Central Avenue in Clayton and answers at (314) 615-7100. If your account is behind, the back tax team at (314) 615-7865 can give the payoff and explain redemption limits.

Two relief programs are worth a question: the county's Senior Property Tax Freeze and the state's Property Tax Credit, nicknamed the Circuit Breaker. If anything is owed, have the title company show the balance on the settlement statement so it is paid out of your proceeds.

Ask your title company which county office records the deed. After closing, shut off your utilities and hand over the keys with any permit paperwork. A current tenant changes the picture, so check the occupancy permit status before the buyer closes.

  • Gather the last occupancy permit, any repair receipts and warranties.
  • Look for open permits on old additions or finished basements.
  • Ask the title company about unpaid city or county charges.

faqs.q: Is an inspection needed to sell in University City?
faqs.a: The city asks sellers to schedule one before listing, and whoever moves in must hold an occupancy permit. A sale inspection runs $80 per unit, on top of the $25 application fee.

faqs.q: What happens if my University City house fails the occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: Corrections are required. A conditional permit at $35 can cover minor items and allows 60 days to finish them, after which an unfinished job can cost the permit.

faqs.q: What is the tax due date for a house in University City?
faqs.a: December 31 of the billing year. Later postmarks add interest and a penalty, so a 2026 balance should be settled through the title company at closing.

faqs.q: When can I appeal my University City assessment?
faqs.a: Appeals go to the Board of Equalization from May 1 through the second Monday in July. The next reassessment year is 2027, and filing opens May 1, 2027.

faqs.q: Do owners or renters dominate University City?
faqs.a: Owners live in 56.2 percent of homes, so landlords are a large share of buyers. Owners put the median value at $306,700.
